Messages.Author: The Fanboy

> I'm not very familiar with the Blood Brothers, how did they come about and
> why are they sterile?

I believe they were created when the !Tremere and Tzimice worked
together on a variant of the ritual that created the Gargoyles. The
ritual that created the Gargoyles had a few limitations that
restricted the usefulness of the new bloodline (it used two vampires
to make one Gargoyle, and the Gargoyles were able to self-replicate --
especially annoying once some of them started to break free from their
masters). The ritual that created the Blood Brothers took existing
vampires, and morphed them into the Blood Brothers. They're generally
made a circle at a time, if I recall correctly. They're sterile as a
result of the ritual. This is especially bad news, since the majority
of the folks who knew how to make them were !Tremere, and they're
mostly all gone. I'm surprised they weren't Scarce AND Sterile.
There again, it'd be really difficult to use Sanguinus in conjunction
with Scarcity.

Fanboy

Mr. Technicality speaking now: =)

Terror Frenzy doesn't actually set range, though for most purposes it acts like
it does (since you can't manuever to close). But if you Terror Frenzy Cailean
or someone with Obtenebration (Shadow Step), then they can still set the range
to long (though Sniper Rifle is hosed since it's equipment). So while the
*real* range-setters (including close-range setters like Storm Sewers and Gang
Tactics) are first-come-first-served (since the range can be "set" only once),
Terror Frenzy doesn't automatically trump any of them if played first (and can
still be played after range is set to cycle).

End of spiel. =)

I think you're overstating it. The limiting factor on combat decks
like this is card slots. You need a zillion Unflinching Persistence
maneuvers to outmaneuver a long-range combat deck (eg Assamite or
Tremere), which leaves not nearly enough slots for beating them up
once you catch them. Plus you need superior Fortitude, which means
your vampires won't be that small, and superior Potence as well if
you want to be able to really hurt people (or else a metric assload
of Disarms).

And after all that, you'll still fail when your opponents have
Fortitude of their own. At least the Assamites can beat that. :-)

On the whole, I'd expect that the Blood Brothers will be as good
at combat as the Brujah, Nosferatu, and Gargoyles, but probably not
really better than any of them. Potence-based combat is always
card-intensive, and the second discipline you use may determine
how well you do against certain other combat decks, but within
combat archetypes you have the same kind of rock/paper/scissors
that you do in the bleed/vote/combat metagame, just because if
you have 15 Unflinchings, 10 Skin of Steel, 15 Torn Signposts,
15 Undead Strengths, 15 Immortal Grapples, and 15 Bum's Rushes,
you only get 5 other cards, and have to leave out the Tastes of
Vitae, the master cards, the Disarms, the Pulled Fangs, and
your deck still only works if you have POT/FOR.

On the other hand, having in-clan Freak Drive is super cool. :-)

Certainly. But it takes up just as many slots as other maneuver cards,

>Decapitate them. Poof.

(head shake)

You can't catch the Assamites if they want to stay at long. They'll be
packing Flash and Pursuit -- and you just won't have that much
Unflinching Persistence available. Most good Assamite decks pack Wakes
and assorted intercept, so your Bum's Rush manuever is gone -- meaning
you'll need two maneuvers.

Trying to catch the Tremere isn't quite as hopeless, but comes with its
own pitfalls: the first being Apportation. It's well worth it to chuck
9,000,000 Apportations in a Tremere deck, since you can dump them
effectively. Staying at close range for a 2nd round gets you Blood to
Water, which means at best, you just traded one of your vamps for one of
theirs; a questionable decision. The second is Thoughts Betrayed, which
will wang up a lot of things for you. The third is the reappearance of
the Thelerity deck in numerous forms -- good luck catching a deck that
has only superior CEL and carries 15 Flash for the maneuver/press/Blood
to Water 2nd round. Worse for you, the Flash is a press to end if they
don't have the cards in hand to survive round 2.

I don't see POT/FOR being any kind of combat trump. It's great for
surviving close range combat where people are trying to punch you for
30, but decks that want to get away have learned how to get away; and
packing enough maneuvers to catch them mean you can't beat up decks that
aren't trying to get away.

Several things.

First, a close-range deck generally does NOT pack permanent maneuvers,
as they're a waste of its time. Long-range decks, on the other hand,
frequently do, even if it's only in the form of Zip Guns which can then
be backed up by transient maneuvers.

Second, a long-range deck gets to play at least one maneuver every
combat. It can afford (in fact, is forced) to overload itself on
maneuvers, because it will be able to cycle them much more freely. A
close-range deck CANNOT afford to put too many maneuvers in, or it will
simply jam up on them and die when faced with non-maneuvering decks.

>I also don't see how Flash + Pursuit is any better than Unflinching
>Persistence + Hidden Strength. Both have highly useable alternates uses. In

Hidden Strength is irrelevant; it doesn't provide a maneuver. Flash and
Pursuit both provide a maneuver, but most importantly, Pursuit provides
additional strikes and can be cycled in that fashion when maneuvers
aren't necessary. If you're a POT deck maneuvering back to close, your
strategy (IG) is painfully obvious, and a long-range deck will gleefully
waste its Pursuits to stay at long range, knowing that the first strike
will be effective.

What this means is that while you have only one source for maneuvers, a
long-range deck can put in twice as many maneuvers as you while still
being able to cycle all its cards freely when it doesn't need to run
away from people.

This assumes you're going up against a big combat deck.

If you *are* going up against a big combat deck, it might be long range
- in which case you can play for maneuver and prevent. Or it's close
range, in which case you can play for prevent.

However, the other case is that you are going up against a non-combat
deck. Or a deck with lots of combat ignore tactics - Elysium, Ex
Nihilo, Majesty. In which case, even if you do go up against them, and
even if you get them to strike, you're only going to take one damage,
most likely.

This is where the problems with cycling quite a few can come in.

How many combat decks will you likely sit at on a table? This is, of
course, a meta-game issue - but in many instances, that's rather low.
If you pile up too high, such that you can cycle against a big combat
deck, you won't be able to cycle fast enough against a small combat
deck.

>need to have a few Skin of Steel to soak big damage.

of such cards, in order to combat many interesting and varied
situations. (For instance, Skin of Steel usually sucks against "I
strike for hands, that's all" deck.)

makes them inherently more usable. If we restrict ourselves to pot/FOR
as a minimum, our smallest vampire is a 6 for that purpose. This, in
part, will stock up your hand with them because you can't weenie the
deck as easily. This makes them inherently less cyclable.

Assuming both decks are still around for damage prevention (that is, the
combat hasn't been ended), an additional strike will almost certainly be
playable. A press to another round will almost certainly be playable.
Prevention of damage - when up against another combat deck - is less
certain. The Assamites are popular now, and the Tremere still get
played.

all. But abstract deck theory such as this HAS to involve the
assumption of a complete lack of knowledge of what you'll be sitting
next to, and the assumption that whatever you sit next to will be
effective at what it does.

harder to win with, you can make a third assumption that you'll most
often be sitting next to NON-combat decks. As such, you want to tailor
the amount of UP in your deck for NON-combat, so you don't get screwed

you can just Rush cross-table to find someone who'll punch you for 2 or

non-combat deck, they can put tons of maneuvers in. They get to play at
least one every combat, no matter WHAT the other deck is playing. Their
permanents are never wasted, as they can always maneuver with the
transients to cycle cards, and save the permanents for when they have no
transients.

Well, there IS the assumption above that combat decks are more difficult
to win with, and this is one reason why (dumping a whole bunch of cards
before range is determined is highly vulnerable to S:CE, unless you can
also play IG or Thoughts Betrayed).

Moving 1 card per combat is significantly more helpful than 0,
obviously. But there's an additional factor available for the CEL deck,
and that's Psyche!. You dump a maneuver and strike hands at long, they
play S:CE, you play Psyche! and restart combat. In situations where
defeating S:CE is not necessary, you can always burn Psyche! for a
press, or to restart against a Carrion Crows/Superior Mettle-playing
vampire.

As I note elsewhere, mono-THA is highly vulnerable to S:CE, although
Perfect Clarity DOES go a long way towards helping that. But mono-THA
makes up for it by being able to ignore Fortitude with impunity,
something almost no combat deck can do.

>Even though we are taking in abstract, I always take the metagame into
>account when finalising a deck. I'll have the base of it on paper but I'll
>often make minor adjustments before I take it with me to playgroup X or to a
>tourney in region Y. If I'm in Sydney I'll add more UP, if I'm down south,
>I'll add more IG.

Hmmm. I've GOT to contend that this may work for you in theory, but in
practice it's absolutely impossible to pull off. On our side of the
pond (USA), even the most 'predictable' players tend to be nearly
impossible to predict -- which makes for a quite interesting (and
challenging) environment to play in. But it also means that trying to
play the metagame can very much get you burnt.

>Given that situation, yes, you can cycle a lot better than I can but in my
>experience there's two kinds of combat. S:CE and something other than just
>hands for 1.

This is definitely where our experience differs. There are so many
different ways to commit combat that I can't even begin to count them
all. My most recent game consisted of decks with, as a combat sideline:

- Carrion Crows/Pushing the Limit/Thrown Gate
- Melee Weapon/Celerity/Blur
- Darkness Within/Arms of the Abyss/strike-hands
- !Ventrue prevent-the-world
- THA/for Theft/Burst/prevent and some Rotschreck

The first two decks would have given you plenty of damage to prevent,
although you might have quickly run out against the first. But sitting
next to the 3rd or 4th deck would have jammed you up on maneuvers
rapidly, and sitting next to the 5th deck would have gotten you dead the
first time you failed to play an IG, since you can't prevent Rotschreck
or Theft.

Two of the decks were, for your purposes, strike-hands for 1. Two of
them were doing unpreventable damage, and one of them was doing too MUCH
damage to easily prevent with UP alone -- it took several Skin of
Steel/etc. to handle properly. And its damage all worked under IG.

There are also many decks who disdain combat entirely, or whose combat
defense is Obedience, bloat, having too many weenies to kill, etc.
These decks will strike-hands for 1 over and over.

>HS is probably a bad example in hindsight, if I was using a lot of UP and
>wanted to press then I should be using Indomitability. Given that my

Nope. You want to be using HS, because it's better than Indomitability
in almost all situations (the ability to spend 1 blood and prevent 2 agg
with a single card and inferior Fortitude is WELL worth it). And your
deck isn't really going to WANT to press, since that's what IG is for,
right?

>opponent is doing absolutely nothing to me in combat, yes, CEL & THA is
>going to cycle a lot better than I am.

If you're playing IG on people, a lot of decks -can't- do anything more
than strike-hands for 1 in combat. That Melee Weapon/Blur deck I cited
above, for example, causes you some difficulty; if you IG it, it hits
you for 1 and you jam up on maneuvers/prevent. If you DON'T IG it, it
Dodges and hits you for 4-6 with a Blur.

>But now you're taking about using Blur, 3 Thefts and a Weather Control which
>all eat up manuver card slots, how do you plan on out manuvering me in the
>first place? Not that that strategy isn't highly unplesant and I'd love to

There's plenty of room in the deck for everything, although you end up
going up to 90 cards and not having much more in the way of bleed
offense other than a couple bleed retainers, Laptops, and Ur-Sluggy or
Al-Ashrad's inherent +1 bleed. On the positive side, your Masters can
be a Minion Tap down to 2-3, so you end up getting a goodly number of
LARGE minions out, and have reasonably effective bloat potential.

>> combat deck.

That's about what I thought a few was, too. When you're Rushing

>> Put 16 UP in yours? You'll die against non-combat.
>
>Non-combat in any playgroup I've played in = S:CE. With 16 Apportations
>you're going to have almost as much trouble as me and you've got little
>chance of doing anything except Weather Controlling both the opposing minion
>and yourself, at least I've got the potential to cycle some non-UP combat
>cards if I can IG.

As mentioned elsewhere, mono-THA *does* lose horribly against S:CE,
although I suppose I could stick some Perfect Clarity in the deck for
Merrill/Aisling to use on their Bum's Rushes.

But non-combat is not always S:CE; a lot of times it's simply Dodge,
Flesh of Marble, or lots of Fortitude. Occasionally it's Masochism,
where they LET you hit them and then prevent. Sometimes it's just Zip
Gun/transient maneuvers, to try to get out of the way.

>If you're playing THA only you are probably going to be at an advantage
>since your vamps are most likely smaller than mine and therefore you have
>more than me. Given the assumption that all I did was Disarm you and not
>actually belt you into Torpor.

The objection was to the "prevent/Disarm/diablerize" idea, yes. It's
much less effective than actually pounding all the blood off someone.

>I usually find that I have a BW, IG and a Sacrament in my hand all at the
>same time. Since I'm the one picking the fights, I tend not to rush a S:CE
>deck without an IG. That Giovanni deck's weakest point is actually the lack

What if it's your predator and bleeding you for about 70 per turn?

This is my point. Sometimes you absolutely, positively, MUST Rush
backwards in your own defense.

>I'm yet to be convinced that CEL + whatever is better than pot/FOR but I
>will concede that with the addition of Weather Control, a THA only deck will
>best pot/FOT most of the time but pot/FOR will perform better against S:CE
>decks than THA.

Celerity is simply the BEST combat support discipline out there. If
you're worried about getting caught at close range, an extensive mix of
Flash/Pursuit/Psyche! will deal with most problems for you; a pot/CEL
deck that carries nothing but Sewer Lids can do lots of damage this way
at 3-6 per round (which also renders Skin of Steel's superior slightly
less useful), and it's perfectly viable for them to include 16+ Flash in
the deck. Against close-range combat, they escape and use the Psyche!
to press, as opposed to the Flash's optional press. Against S:CE, they
have Psyche! to restart combat and plenty of Flash to get back to long.
Against wacko combat, they have multiple presses/maneuvers/restarts
available as necessary, although other long-range combat will give them
some trouble.

In the above described deck, I'd consider using:

16 Flash
6 Pursuit
8 Psyche!

although I might swap out the 6 Pursuit for 6 Side Strike, depending on
whether or not I was REALLY worried about long-range combat being
around.

>Now that I am actually slowly acquiring some Apportations. WC + Apportation
>+ Theft sounds highly unplesant, I'll have to give it a go.

It really offends the heavy Fortitude players, I'll say that. The
Ventrue definitely get kind of pissed off when Blythe wanders in,
torporizes your vampire, and ends up only down 1 blood. A lot of quick
math is called for to determine whether you should play the WC at
superior or inferior -- vamps with 6 blood, for example, can be dealt
with by WC/theft/press/theft/press, and while it's more intensive on the
Thefts and presses, it's also a lot easier on your vamp.
